newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU grapples with paradox of flexibility.
newsitem.headline: EU grapples with paradox of flexibility.

text.p: With no apparent regard to the paradox, the European Union is continuing a major reworking of its treaties with one aim -- to set rigid rules for just how flexible the bloc can become.
"No one wants to see an 'a la carte' Europe," said Nikolaus van der Pas, spokesman for the European Commission. "But at the same time it is important that we have a framework for flexibility."

Van der Pas was speaking on Wednesday after the Commission met for the first time this year and also launched an internal examination of the inter-governmental conference (IGC), the re-working of the 15-nation bloc's treaties.
A new European treaty is vital if the EU is to expand and take in the more than a dozen countries clamouring for membership, but nations are divided on what shape or form the future bloc should take.
Pressed by an increasingly Euro-sceptical Britain, the theme of the IGC is flexibility -- allowing individual countries to decide to what extent they should embrace European unity.
But Germany and France are also pressing for the future to be more formally legislated and are insisting that opt-out clauses should be the exception rather than the rule.
The task of negotiating the new treaty has fallen to the Netherlands, which, under the EU's rotating presidency, also steered the current Maastricht Treaty to conclusion in 1991.
In the Hague on Tuesday, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok insisted he would press ahead with reforms despite the issue likely to become a cornerstone a British general election later this year.
"We are not just sitting back and waiting for what will happen after the (British) elections," he said. "We cannot afford the luxury of losing time."
Van der Pas said the European Commissioners on Wednesday opened their discussion on two key areas of the new treaty -- flexibility and the shake-up of the EU's institutions.
"They were, in effect, discussing their own demise," said one Commission official, referring to plans to slash the executive which critics argue is too unweildy.
At present, each EU member country nominates at least one of its nationals to the Commission and President Jacques Santer has 19 "cabinet" members -- more than many governments.

Germany has made no secret of its wish to see the Commission slashed to 12 regardless of the EU taking in more members and also wants the Commission president to be able to handpick his colleagues from a short-list prepared by member states.
Van der Pas said the commissioners reached no conclusions following their discussions on Wednesday but were expected to have an initial report ready for an EU ministerial meeting on January 20.
"It was a very general, introductory debate," said van der Pas. "You cannot say there were agreements or disagreements, just discussion."
